## Current scope, review outcome, drift and progress

This revision response supersedes the first submission for candidate selection. Initial audit/counts and the exact reviewed v1 objects remain historical records in JSON; round2 is the current packet. No shared registry, manifest, runtime, original question, source module or other topic was edited.

Scope: Peptic ulcer, H. pylori, nonvariceal upper GI bleeding, gastric outlet obstruction, gastroparesis and post-gastrectomy benign physiology.

Boundary: Gastric tumors belong to stomach-neoplasia. Bariatric-anatomy complications belong to bariatric-metabolic. Portal hypertensive bleeding belongs to liver-benign-portal-infection.

Priority: high. Bleeding and obstruction offer central diagnosis, intervention and rescue decisions.

Independent review: [docs/research/question-topic-stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility-review-20261111.json](question-topic-stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility-review-20261111.json), SHA-256 6bcd5a20303d363a2945f129cb097c332488b84450474af60ef89463a0c7fa76. Verdicts: 9 PASS, 13 REVISE, 0 FAIL. Every returned item received one attempt. Nine PASS questions are unchanged; eight v2 revisions are candidates; five attempts are parked. All clinical material remains needs_clinician_review.

Current preview: 17 single-node cases / 17 scored questions / 17 concepts (6 existing meanings reused, 11 new meanings). Three revised objectives introduce distinct new concept identities in this round. There are no current multipart cases. The original five multipart v1 cases are retained only for audit; no returned or parked companion can block a PASS node.

Three exact PASS nodes were isolated from mixed cases: recurrent-bleeding-repeat, perforation-imaging and late-meal-acarbose. Clinical wording, question IDs, concept IDs, patient profiles, choices and feedback remain exact. Case IDs and summaries change only to isolate the node; final completion metadata is added where schema validity requires it. Six originally standalone PASS cases remain full-object exact. Full original cases/nodes remain exact in reviewed-v1 exports and JSON.

Planning baseline: manifest v9 / 145 acceptance rows / 1,151 cases / 1,462 nodes / 610 concepts. The five parked v2 definitions are preserved as audit-only attempts with their actual failed author gates and item-specific responses. They are absent from current QuestionVariant, case, timing and order exports. A reused concept identity can remain when a different retained question still tests it. The small-duodenal-repair attempt has no defensible unique key between patch and no patch, so its attempted first-option flag is not a valid scored key and is never exposed through a preview release.

### Rank 1: Recurrent bleeding and sequential rescue

Decision: Interpret initial success, fresh recurrence, acquired access, current support trajectory and completion results; select repeat EGD, arterial rescue or operative rescue.

Raw evidence: Fresh versus old blood; actual treatment record; targetability and residual flow. Closest error: Treat recurrence as failure, or a performed procedure as achieved control. Consequence: Delay or prematurely escalate hemorrhage control.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-repeat, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-embolization, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-operation, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-old-blood Existing identities: concept.n2r3.ulcer-recurrence-rescue-sequence, concept.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.endoscopic-hemostasis-modality, concept.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.endoscopic-hemostasis-modality.v2, concept.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.high-risk-stigmata-endoscopic-hemostasis, concept.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.high-risk-stigmata-endoscopic-hemostasis.v2

### Rank 2: H. pylori persistence and eradication

Decision: Reconcile assay preparation, prior regimen and susceptibility before testing or prescribing.

Raw evidence: Actual antibiotic/PPI/bismuth exposure; assay identity and prior therapy. Closest error: Treat post-cure IgG or use empiric resistance-prone salvage. Consequence: Unnecessary antibiotics or another failed eradication.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-nonserologic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-preparation, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-salvage-bqt, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-resistance Existing identities: concept.h-pylori-ulcer.active-infection-testing, concept.h-pylori-ulcer.test-of-cure-plan, concept.n2.hpylori-antibody-after-valid-cure-test, concept.n2r2.h-pylori-cure-test-medication-calendar

### Rank 3: Structural outlet assessment before motility attribution

Decision: Identify whether prior acquisition/sample location actually excludes a structural outlet problem.

Raw evidence: Scope termination, sampled site, CT thickening and actual contrast passage. Closest error: Treat retained food or diabetes as proof of gastroparesis. Consequence: Miss an unassessed structural lesion.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-obstruction Existing identities: concept.n1.gastric-emptying-structural-prerequisite

### Rank 4: Perforation imaging, repair and access

Decision: Choose the next investigation and match source-control scope/access to observed defect and physiology.

Raw evidence: Negative radiograph versus acute examination; measured viable defect; actual resuscitation trajectory. Closest error: Exclude a leak from one film, overoperate a small defect, or use a stable-patient access plan during worsening support. Consequence: Delayed or disproportionate source control.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-ct, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-source-control, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-primary-repair, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-access Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

### Rank 5: Gastric-emptying acquisition and confounding

Decision: Decide whether a report is sufficient for a current intrinsic motility diagnosis and intervention planning.

Raw evidence: Actual imaging duration, drug/glucose exposure and interval symptom response. Closest error: Accept a normal short study or a confounded complete study as conclusive. Consequence: Wrong diagnostic label or premature invasive treatment.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-four-hour, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-short-study, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-confounders Existing identities: concept.gastroparesis.confirmatory-gastric-emptying-scintigraphy

### Rank 6: PPI phase after hemostasis

Decision: Keep current response separate from pretreatment risk and course completion.

Raw evidence: Index hemostasis and the actual elapsed phase despite a later dry view. Closest error: Downstage early because bleeding stopped or confuse a different old episode with the current lesion. Consequence: Inappropriate treatment intensity.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-ppi, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-healing-ppi Existing identities: concept.n2.ulcer-posthemostasis-acid-suppression

### Rank 7: Ulcer stigmata and exact treatment site

Decision: Interpret raised versus flat findings and act at the correct site.

Raw evidence: Site-specific observed ulcer floors after lavage, not generic risk labels. Closest error: Treat a dark flat mark or wrong ulcer because the field is dry. Consequence: Leave a high-risk target untreated.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-high-risk, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-low-risk, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-vessel-modality Existing identities: concept.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.high-risk-stigmata-endoscopic-hemostasis, concept.peptic-ulcer-bleeding.high-risk-stigmata-endoscopic-hemostasis.v2

### Rank 8: Secondary-prevention antiplatelet after controlled bleeding

Decision: Use actual aspirin indication with achieved control and ulcer protection.

Raw evidence: Prior infarction versus a merely preventive medication; current hemostatic course. Closest error: Wait for complete healing or automatically change antiplatelet identity. Consequence: Avoidable interruption of secondary prevention.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.aspirin-secondary, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.aspirin-ppi Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

### Rank 9: Gastric nutrition and route-specific response

Decision: Match diet and feeding access to actual retained food and delivered nutrition.

Raw evidence: Food-form tolerance; failed gastric feeds; successful delivered postpyloric trial. Closest error: Use generic high-fiber advice or equate gastric failure with intestinal failure. Consequence: Ongoing inadequate intake or avoidable parenteral exposure.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-diet, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-jejunal, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-parenteral Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

### Rank 10: Post-gastrectomy early and late meal responses

Decision: Use timing, measured glucose and treatment response to choose diet or a medication stage.

Raw evidence: Early normal-glucose vasomotor/GI symptoms versus later measured hypoglycemia after a real dietary trial. Closest error: Conflate every weak spell with hypoglycemia or apply a prokinetic to the opposite physiology. Consequence: Persistent episodes or inappropriate treatment escalation.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.dumping-early, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.dumping-diet, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.dumping-late, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.dumping-acarbose, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.dumping-octreotide Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

### Rank 11: Prokinetic selection after a movement adverse effect

Decision: Recognize a historical drug event and distinguish a motor target from nausea relief.

Raw evidence: Prior neck/eye movement pattern, drug chronology and current QT/interaction review. Closest error: Reuse the familiar drug after a resolved reaction or substitute symptom relief for motility treatment. Consequence: Re-exposure adverse effect or unaddressed motor target.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-prokinetic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.metoclopramide-dystonia, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.metoclopramide-reaction, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-antiemetic-target Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

### Rank 12: Hypergastrinemia after prior ulcer surgery

Decision: Interpret a hormone in its acid/drug/reconstruction context before tumor-directed testing.

Raw evidence: On-PPI hormone result, nonacidic aspirate and incomplete resection map. Closest error: Call retained antrum or gastrinoma from a label or isolated hormone. Consequence: False attribution or unsafe preparation.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gastrin-confounding, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gastrin-surgery, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.ppi-withdrawal Existing identities: concept.retained-antrum.recognition

### Rank 13: Benign pyloric obstruction treatment after diagnosis

Decision: Determine when medical/endoscopic treatment versus operative relief is appropriate for a fully characterized benign lesion.

Raw evidence: Verified etiology, lesion length/tissue features, prior response and nutritional course would be required. Closest error: Rank dilation, stent and bypass from an unverified generic rule. Consequence: An unsupported procedure key.

Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-obstruction, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.goo-ranking-uncertain, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.goo-response-factors Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

### Rank 14: Afferent-loop and bile-reflux post-gastrectomy decisions

Decision: Build future mechanism-directed cases only after verifying adequate anatomy, acquisition and treatment evidence.

Raw evidence: Reconstruction limb map, acquired imaging and observed response would be required. Closest error: Use a syndrome label as a substitute for a consequential action. Consequence: Unsupported or merely recall-level postoperative teaching.

Claims: Research gap only; no supported clinical key asserted. Existing identities: No relevant active identity in the assigned inventory.

Patient: Mara Ellis, 53, Female. Complaint: Recurrent ulcer review. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.recurrent-ulcer-gastrin.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 53-year-old woman, attends clinic to review recurrent marginal ulceration after a Billroth II operation performed for peptic ulcer disease.

Current update: The operative summary calls the procedure an antrectomy, but its specimen map is absent. Fasting gastrin was elevated while she was taking omeprazole. Gastric aspirate obtained during that endoscopy had pH 6. The marginal ulcer was still present.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which diagnostic plan should be arranged next for {patientName}'s elevated gastrin?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Review reconstruction anatomy and obtain supervised gastrin/acid assessment [KEY] ? The drug exposure and nonacidic aspirate prevent the gastrin result from proving inappropriate acid secretion. Reconstruct the prior operation and arrange specialist-supervised assessment; retained antrum remains a postsurgical alternative.
2. Repeat gastrin and perform secretin testing during current PPI therapy ? Repeating the hormone or adding a provocative test during acid suppression does not resolve the physiologic confounding represented here.
3. Obtain receptor PET/CT and pancreatic endoscopic ultrasonography ? Localization does not establish why gastrin is elevated. The current biochemical record and prior surgery need interpretation before a tumor-location strategy.

Explanation: Interpret gastrin together with gastric acidity, acid-suppressive treatment and prior reconstruction. The current result does not establish gastrinoma. Arrange a supervised assessment rather than abrupt PPI withdrawal during active ulcer disease.

Reasoning 1: An elevated hormone in a nonacidic stomach during PPI treatment is not evidence of unopposed acid hypersecretion. Reasoning 2: Select a physiologic/reconstruction assessment before tumor-directed testing; protect ongoing ulcer treatment.

Closest error: secretin. Deciding observation: Gastrin was measured during omeprazole exposure and the aspirate was nonacidic; the resection map is incomplete. Consequence: A false tumor attribution or unsafe drug withdrawal can lead to inappropriate testing and ulcer complications.

Counterfactual: If supervised acid testing establishes interpretable inappropriate hypergastrinemia and the reconstruction excludes retained antral tissue, additional provocative biochemical testing can become appropriate. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gastrin-safe-assessment.secretin. Deletion: Without treatment/acid observations, immediate biochemical escalation becomes plausible; without the surgery history, reconstructing the operation adds no value.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Removed the old phrase residual antral mucosa and the answer-label match. All choices are diagnostic plans. The two-part key is comparable in scope to the two named alternatives; pH is necessary evidence, not a supplied interpretation.

If supervised acid testing establishes interpretable inappropriate hypergastrinemia and the reconstruction excludes retained antral tissue, additional provocative biochemical testing can become appropriate.

Patient: Nora Chen, 46, Female. Complaint: Ulcer treatment follow-up. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.persistent-ulcer-infection.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 46-year-old woman, attends clinic after treatment of an uncomplicated duodenal ulcer. She completed PPI, amoxicillin and clarithromycin, but intermittent epigastric discomfort persists.

Current update: A stool antigen specimen collected six weeks after antibiotics was negative while she was still taking omeprazole. Later serum IgG was positive. There has been no recurrent bleeding, weight loss or vomiting; no additional antibiotics or bismuth have been taken.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which testing plan should be arranged next to assess {patientName}'s H. pylori status?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Urea breath testing after PPI washout [KEY] ? The prior negative specimen was obtained during acid suppression; antibody positivity cannot settle whether infection persists. A prepared active-infection test addresses the remaining question.
2. Repeat serum H. pylori IgG testing ? Another antibody result will not distinguish persistent infection from prior exposure after treatment.
3. Repeat upper endoscopy with gastric biopsies ? Biopsy-based testing can assess infection, but this stable uncomplicated-ulcer follow-up has a preparation problem and no supplied separate indication for repeat invasive examination.

Explanation: Use an active-infection assay with appropriate preparation. A negative on-PPI specimen and positive post-treatment IgG do not establish cure or persistence. PPI must be withheld for two weeks and antibiotics/bismuth for four weeks before eradication testing.

Reasoning 1: Identify the on-PPI negative as insufficient and the antibody as evidence that cannot establish persistence. Reasoning 2: Choose a prepared noninvasive active assay rather than repeat the uninformative assay or add invasive evaluation.

Closest error: endoscopy. Deciding observation: Medication exposure explains a valid uncertainty; there is no independent structural or alarm indication for endoscopy. Consequence: Calling cure or prescribing another course from these results risks missed infection or unnecessary antibiotic exposure.

Counterfactual: If vomiting and a new irregular outlet lesion accompanied the unresolved tests, upper endoscopy with biopsy would become the priority. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.active-infection-recheck.endoscopy. Deletion: Remove the on-PPI collection condition and the premise for repeat active testing changes. Alarm negatives retain their job of ranking invasive reassessment.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Replaced FIT and fasting gastrin foils with competing infection-assessment routes. No task word uniquely names breath testing. The PPI observation establishes an interference problem without announcing the assay choice.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three specific investigations for current infection-status uncertainty.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: Identify the on-PPI negative as insufficient and the antibody as evidence that cannot establish persistence. Then Choose a prepared noninvasive active assay rather than repeat the uninformative assay or add invasive evaluation.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted: reconcile acquisition conditions and choose the proportional next investigation.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: Medication exposure explains a valid uncertainty; there is no independent structural or alarm indication for endoscopy. If vomiting and a new irregular outlet lesion accompanied the unresolved tests, upper endoscopy with biopsy would become the priority.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.active-infection-recheck.serology: temptation Use the positive assay as the more convincing of two discordant tests. Why not here: Another antibody result will not distinguish persistent infection from prior exposure after treatment. Reasonable counterfactual: A prior-exposure question rather than eradication assessment is being studied; this is not a cure test. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-nonserologic.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.active-infection-recheck.endoscopy: temptation Resolve test disagreement by escalating directly to invasive sampling. Why not here: Biopsy-based testing can assess infection, but this stable uncomplicated-ulcer follow-up has a preparation problem and no supplied separate indication for repeat invasive examination. Reasonable counterfactual: A new alarm feature or a structural lesion independently requires endoscopy and appropriate biopsy. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-test-of-cure, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-preparation.

Patient: Owen Marsh, 54, Male. Complaint: Ulcer test scheduling. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.cure-collection-calendar.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old man, attends clinic to schedule a stool antigen test after H. pylori eradication therapy.

Current update: Eradication antibiotics ended eight weeks ago. Omeprazole ended three weeks ago, and he has taken no bismuth. A later amoxicillin course for a dental infection ended four days ago. The listed medicines remain stopped.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which collection date should be used for {patientName}'s stool antigen test?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Collect the stool specimen 24 days from today [KEY] ? Four more days have elapsed since the later antibiotic course; another 24 days completes the four-week antibiotic-free interval. The PPI interval has already been met.
2. Collect the stool specimen 14 days from today ? This follows the familiar two-week interval but leaves only 18 days since the later antibiotic course.
3. Collect the stool specimen at today's clinic visit ? The remote eradication date and completed PPI hold do not negate the recent antibiotic exposure.

Explanation: Use the most recent relevant exposure: four days since the later antibiotic plus 24 more days equals four weeks. The three-week PPI hold already exceeds the two-week preparation interval. These clinical preparation intervals are separate from runtime laboratory waits.

Reasoning 1: The later dental antibiotic resets the antibiotic-free interval even though eradication therapy ended much earlier. Reasoning 2: Reconcile the completed PPI interval with the remaining antibiotic interval and select the offered date.

Closest error: day14. Deciding observation: The later antibiotic ended four days ago, while PPI ended three weeks ago. Consequence: An early negative specimen could be accepted incorrectly as eradication.

Counterfactual: If the dental antibiotic had ended fourteen days ago, collection fourteen days from today would meet the same rules. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.cure-calendar.day14. Deletion: Deleting the later antibiotic changes the answer to today; deleting the PPI record leaves necessary preparation uncertain.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Every option is the same specimen collection with a different date and identical wait-profile scope. No antibody backstory, explanatory qualifier or treatment-choice distraction remains.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Specimen collection dates, not antibiotic treatment decisions.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: The later dental antibiotic resets the antibiotic-free interval even though eradication therapy ended much earlier. Then Reconcile the completed PPI interval with the remaining antibiotic interval and select the offered date.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted: the credible error is applying a two-week interval to all drugs or using the original eradication end date.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: The later antibiotic ended four days ago, while PPI ended three weeks ago. If the dental antibiotic had ended fourteen days ago, collection fourteen days from today would meet the same rules.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.cure-calendar.day14: temptation Apply the PPI interval to the later antibiotic. - Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.cure-calendar.today: temptation Count preparation from eradication treatment while overlooking later medicines. Patient: Simon Park, 55, Male. Complaint: Conflicting ulcer tests. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.cure-serology-disagreement.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside laboratory reports positive H. pylori IgG following ulcer treatment.

Current update: The earlier stool antigen test was negative eight weeks after eradication antibiotics. PPI had been stopped for three weeks; there had been no antibiotics or bismuth for six weeks. Epigastric symptoms have resolved.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which H. pylori treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s current results?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Do not prescribe another eradication course [KEY] ? The active-infection specimen met preparation intervals. Later antibody positivity does not establish persistent infection requiring antibiotics.
2. Prescribe bismuth-based quadruple eradication therapy ? BQT treats established infection; IgG positivity does not establish persistence after this adequately prepared negative active test.
3. Prescribe levofloxacin-based triple eradication therapy ? Neither persistent infection nor levofloxacin susceptibility is demonstrated by antibody positivity.

Explanation: A correctly prepared active-infection test has a different role from antibody serology. Preserve the supported cure assessment rather than prescribe another course for IgG positivity.

Reasoning 1: Check every relevant medication interval before accepting the negative active assay, then distinguish antibody persistence from current infection. Reasoning 2: Avoid an unnecessary eradication course.

Closest error: bqt. Deciding observation: The earlier active test is negative with adequate preparation; the later positive test is antibody-based. Consequence: Unnecessary antibiotics create adverse effects and avoidable selection pressure.

Counterfactual: A positive prepared active assay after prior clarithromycin failure, with no prior BQT, would support BQT. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.valid-cure-antibody.bqt. Deletion: Without preparation data, the negative test cannot carry this conclusion and re-evaluation would be needed.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Replaced abstract retain-the-conclusion wording with actual prescribing plans. No generic individualized key. The symptom resolution is supportive context, not proof of eradication; medication and assay identity determine the answer.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three current antibiotic-prescribing decisions.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: Check every relevant medication interval before accepting the negative active assay, then distinguish antibody persistence from current infection. Then Avoid an unnecessary eradication course.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted: the trap is privileging a newer positive assay over a properly prepared active test.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: The earlier active test is negative with adequate preparation; the later positive test is antibody-based. A positive prepared active assay after prior clarithromycin failure, with no prior BQT, would support BQT.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.valid-cure-antibody.bqt: temptation Treat the latest positive laboratory label as the decisive result. Why not here: BQT treats established infection; IgG positivity does not establish persistence after this adequately prepared negative active test. Reasonable counterfactual: A prepared active-infection test is positive and prior-regimen history supports BQT. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-nonserologic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-salvage-bqt.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.valid-cure-antibody.levofloxacin: temptation Assume a positive follow-up antibody requires a different antibiotic family. Why not here: Neither persistent infection nor levofloxacin susceptibility is demonstrated by antibody positivity. Reasonable counterfactual: Persistent active infection and susceptibility-guided salvage support that regimen. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-nonserologic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-resistance.

Full-sequence check: Standalone; no prior calendar question teaches that this particular specimen was valid.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-nonserologic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-preparation, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-test-of-cure, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-resistance, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.hp-salvage-bqt. Patient: Elena Ward, 49, Female. Complaint: Vomiting after meals. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.vomiting-and-nutrition.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old woman with diabetes, attends clinic for persistent nausea, early satiety and vomiting after solid meals.

Current update: Endoscopy documented a traversable pylorus and duodenum, with no narrowing or obstructing lesion. A solid-meal emptying study was reported within the laboratory range at two hours; the acquisition log ends at that time. Glucose was controlled and no motility-altering medicines were used during testing.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which investigation should be arranged next for {patientName}'s persistent meal-related vomiting?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Solid-meal scintigraphy with four-hour acquisition [KEY] ? The prior study did not acquire the later measurement. A directly measured four-hour solid-meal protocol can resolve the remaining emptying question.
2. Repeat endoscopy with repeat pyloric inspection ? An adequate recent examination already addressed an outlet lesion. Repeating that structural assessment does not supply the missing emptying acquisition.
3. High-resolution esophageal manometry with impedance ? The unresolved evidence concerns gastric emptying rather than esophageal propulsion or passage at the esophagogastric junction.

Explanation: Separate an adequate outlet examination from an incomplete emptying acquisition. A two-hour report cannot supply an unacquired four-hour measurement. Use a standardized solid-meal protocol with direct later imaging.

Reasoning 1: The outlet was examined adequately, but the normal two-hour result does not establish the later emptying result. Reasoning 2: Choose the investigation that fills the remaining physiologic evidence gap.

Closest error: repeat-egds. Deciding observation: The acquisition log ends at two hours while the outlet examination is complete. Consequence: Prematurely closing the emptying question can mislabel persistent symptoms or trigger inappropriate treatment.

Counterfactual: If the endoscope had stopped before an irregular pyloric lesion and sampled only proximal mucosa, repeat targeted endoscopy would take priority. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.complete-emptying-acquisition.repeat-egds. Deletion: Deleting the acquisition log makes the word normal misleadingly conclusive; deleting the outlet details leaves repeat endoscopy reasonable.

### question.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.motility-diet.v1

Kind: new. Concept: concept.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gastroparesis-diet-selection.v1; relation new_meaning; previous none. Exact after SHA-256: a38399c9bf27057022836e360ade5260f6bd521fa4b477d78186f9070330a066. Status: needs_clinician_review.

Before: [] (explicitly new; no existing item is invented).

Other consolidated records: none. Their complete before contexts remain in JSON exactInputs.

Patient: Elena Ward, 49, Female. Complaint: Vomiting after meals. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.vomiting-and-nutrition.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 49-year-old woman with diabetes, attends clinic for persistent nausea, early satiety and vomiting after solid meals.

Prior visible sequence (must be considered with this task):
- question.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.complete-emptying-acquisition.v1: Endoscopy documented a traversable pylorus and duodenum, with no narrowing or obstructing lesion. A solid-meal emptying study was reported within the laboratory range at two hours; the acquisition log ends at that time. Glucose was controlled and no motility-altering medicines were used during testing. Task: Which investigation should be arranged next for {patientName}'s persistent meal-related vomiting? Feedback: Separate an adequate outlet examination from an incomplete emptying acquisition. A two-hour report cannot supply an unacquired four-hour measurement. Use a standardized solid-meal protocol with direct later imaging.

Current update: The later standardized study directly measures delayed solid emptying at four hours. Her diet log shows large raw-vegetable meals and added bran for diabetes care. She vomits recognizable solids but retains smooth soups and blended meals. She has not had a structured nutrition intervention.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which nutrition prescription best fits {patientName}'s current oral tolerance?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Small low-fat, low-fiber meals with blended foods [KEY] ? This plan reduces the solid and residue burden while using the foods she can retain to sustain intake.
2. Small whole-grain meals with added bran supplements ? Generic high-fiber advice does not address the retained rough solids that now limit this patient's intake.
3. Small high-fat meals with dense solid supplements ? Concentrating solid calories with fat does not match the low-fat, easier-to-process dietary approach or her observed food tolerance.

Explanation: Dietary treatment must fit both the emptying disorder and actual food tolerance. Use small, lower-fat and lower-fiber meals, with blended foods as needed, before concluding that oral nutrition has failed.

Reasoning 1: Whole solids are poorly retained while blended intake remains possible; a standard high-fiber diet is not serving this new physiology. Reasoning 2: Select a gastric-tolerance nutrition plan rather than maximize fiber or solid calorie density.

Closest error: fiber. Deciding observation: Retained recognizable solids and successful blended intake occur with documented delayed solid emptying. Consequence: An ill-matched diet can perpetuate vomiting and inadequate nutrition.

Counterfactual: If delayed emptying were not present and the actual dietary problem were fiber-responsive bowel symptoms with preserved food tolerance, the whole-grain/bran plan could become reasonable. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.motility-diet.fiber. Deletion: Without the diet log and food-form response, the item becomes simple dietary recall; those observations defeat the credible generic diabetes-diet error.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: All options are small-meal prescriptions of similar scope; no uniquely comprehensive feeding-access key. The task does not say low residue. The known diagnosis is appropriate because the scored task is treatment.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three oral dietary prescriptions before oral nutrition has been optimized.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: Whole solids are poorly retained while blended intake remains possible; a standard high-fiber diet is not serving this new physiology. Then Select a gastric-tolerance nutrition plan rather than maximize fiber or solid calorie density.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted, with a residual risk of being too familiar for PGY-2/3; independent review must assess the fiber-versus-gastric-tolerance error.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: Retained recognizable solids and successful blended intake occur with documented delayed solid emptying. If delayed emptying were not present and the actual dietary problem were fiber-responsive bowel symptoms with preserved food tolerance, the whole-grain/bran plan could become reasonable.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.motility-diet.fiber: temptation Continue a usual diabetes-oriented high-fiber strategy despite the changed gastric problem. Why not here: Generic high-fiber advice does not address the retained rough solids that now limit this patient's intake. Reasonable counterfactual: An appropriate dietary problem calls for more fiber and the patient tolerates it; this is not the current gastric plan. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-diet.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.motility-diet.fat: temptation Treat the nutritional risk by increasing calorie density without considering gastric processing. Why not here: Concentrating solid calories with fat does not match the low-fat, easier-to-process dietary approach or her observed food tolerance. Reasonable counterfactual: A different nutrition problem and demonstrated fat tolerance justify that prescription; no such evidence is given here. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-diet.

Full-sequence check: Prior feedback establishes test adequacy, not diet composition. This feedback does not name the next node's feeding route.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-diet, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-four-hour. Field/choice mappings: JSON proposals[].statementMapping and source ledger statementMappings. Clinical boundary: Government diet guidance is broad; calorie, fluid and diabetes medication adjustments remain outside the keyed objective.

Patient: Elena Ward, 49, Female. Complaint: Vomiting after meals. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.vomiting-and-nutrition.v1.

Prior visible sequence (must be considered with this task):
- question.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.complete-emptying-acquisition.v1: Endoscopy documented a traversable pylorus and duodenum, with no narrowing or obstructing lesion. A solid-meal emptying study was reported within the laboratory range at two hours; the acquisition log ends at that time. Glucose was controlled and no motility-altering medicines were used during testing. Task: Which investigation should be arranged next for {patientName}'s persistent meal-related vomiting? Feedback: Separate an adequate outlet examination from an incomplete emptying acquisition. A two-hour report cannot supply an unacquired four-hour measurement. Use a standardized solid-meal protocol with direct later imaging.
- question.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.motility-diet.v1: The later standardized study directly measures delayed solid emptying at four hours. Her diet log shows large raw-vegetable meals and added bran for diabetes care. She vomits recognizable solids but retains smooth soups and blended meals. She has not had a structured nutrition intervention. Task: Which nutrition prescription best fits {patientName}'s current oral tolerance? Feedback: Dietary treatment must fit both the emptying disorder and actual food tolerance. Use small, lower-fat and lower-fiber meals, with blended foods as needed, before concluding that oral nutrition has failed.

Current update: At a later outside admission, dietitian-guided oral changes and medical therapy still did not meet her nutritional needs. Gastric tube feeds caused repeated regurgitation. During a nasojejunal trial, the prescribed feed was delivered and retained, with no recurrent vomiting or abdominal distension.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which longer-term nutrition route best fits {patientName}'s observed feeding response?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Jejunal enteral feeding access [KEY] ? The trial demonstrates that bypassing the stomach can deliver the prescribed nutrition. It supports an enteral route beyond the dysfunctional stomach.
2. Gastric enteral feeding access ? This places the feed in the compartment that repeatedly regurgitated it; permanent access does not itself correct that observed tolerance problem.
3. Central venous parenteral nutrition ? The record demonstrates a usable enteral route. Parenteral nutrition is not required simply because gastric emptying is severely impaired.

Explanation: The decisive evidence is successful delivery and retention during the postpyloric trial after oral and gastric routes failed. Consider jejunal access; parenteral nutrition remains a fallback when adequate enteral support cannot be delivered.

Reasoning 1: The stomach has failed as a feeding reservoir, but the intestinal trial demonstrates adequate enteral delivery. Reasoning 2: Choose durable jejunal rather than gastric or intravenous feeding.

Closest error: parenteral. Deciding observation: The prescribed postpyloric feed was actually delivered and retained, not merely planned. Consequence: Ignoring the response can cause recurrent gastric-feed failure or avoidable central-line nutrition exposure.

Counterfactual: If appropriately placed postpyloric feeding repeatedly failed to provide nutrition and enteral delivery could not be achieved, parenteral nutrition would become reasonable. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.jejunal-nutrition.parenteral. Deletion: Remove actual trial delivery/tolerance and the long-term route is insufficiently established; a proposed trial would not prove success.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: All labels are concrete feeding routes. No generic individualized plan or uniquely complete key. Successful trial language is essential response evidence, not permission that an untested procedure is feasible.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three longer-term nutrition-access strategies after demonstrated treatment responses.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: The stomach has failed as a feeding reservoir, but the intestinal trial demonstrates adequate enteral delivery. Then Choose durable jejunal rather than gastric or intravenous feeding.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted: distinguish gastric failure from intestinal failure using what nutrition was actually delivered.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: The prescribed postpyloric feed was actually delivered and retained, not merely planned. If appropriately placed postpyloric feeding repeatedly failed to provide nutrition and enteral delivery could not be achieved, parenteral nutrition would become reasonable.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.jejunal-nutrition.gastric: temptation Choose the simpler common feeding tube without using the trial response. Why not here: This places the feed in the compartment that repeatedly regurgitated it; permanent access does not itself correct that observed tolerance problem. Reasonable counterfactual: The stomach can retain adequate feeds and the primary limitation is safe oral delivery. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-jejunal.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.jejunal-nutrition.parenteral: temptation Equate failure of oral and gastric feeding with failure of the whole intestinal route. Why not here: The record demonstrates a usable enteral route. Parenteral nutrition is not required simply because gastric emptying is severely impaired. Reasonable counterfactual: Adequate postpyloric nutrition cannot be achieved or enteral feeding is contraindicated. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-parenteral.

Full-sequence check: Diet feedback did not name jejunal or parenteral routes. The later admission supplies new consequential response data; no future findings were used earlier.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-jejunal, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-parenteral. Field/choice mappings: JSON proposals[].statementMapping and source ledger statementMappings. Clinical boundary: Single adequate government source; access technique and exact nutrition targets require clinician selection and are not tested.

Patient: Lena Grant, 58, Female. Complaint: Vomiting test review. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.confounded-emptying-record.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside delayed gastric-emptying report before an invasive pyloric-treatment consultation.

Current update: The outside study used a solid meal with four-hour imaging. Its medication record shows oxycodone before the meal, and glucose was well above that laboratory's testing target. CT and endoscopy had shown no outlet lesion. Since the postoperative opioid course ended and glucose returned to the usual range, vomiting has become much less frequent.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which investigation should be arranged next before {patientName}'s pyloric treatment decision?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Repeat solid-meal scintigraphy under controlled preparation [KEY] ? The acquisition duration was adequate, but drug/metabolic exposures and interval improvement raise a different validity problem. Reassess emptying without the documented confounders.
2. Endoscopic measurement of pyloric distensibility ? A pyloric measurement does not establish that the confounded emptying abnormality persists after reversible factors change.
3. Repeat contrast examination of the gastric outlet ? The reviewed CT and endoscopy addressed an outlet lesion, and no new obstructive pattern is supplied. The unresolved discrepancy is physiologic test preparation and interval response.

Explanation: A four-hour duration does not remove medication or glucose confounding. The interval improvement makes persistence clinically important to reassess before an invasive pyloric decision. Use controlled preparation rather than a universal drug-hold or glucose cutoff invented for the case.

Reasoning 1: The test measured emptying during opioid exposure and excess glucose; the subsequent improvement is evidence against treating that result as a fixed current phenotype. Reasoning 2: Obtain an interpretable current emptying measurement before a pylorus-specific selection test.

Closest error: pylorus. Deciding observation: The exposure record conflicts with the current untreated symptom course despite adequate imaging duration. Consequence: Premature invasive treatment can target a reversible or no-longer-present abnormality.

Counterfactual: If repeated properly prepared studies showed continuing delay despite optimized medical care, a pyloric distensibility assessment could become reasonable during specialist procedural evaluation. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.confounded-scan.pylorus. Deletion: Deleting the medication/glucose record and interval improvement turns repeat testing into an unsupported delay. The four-hour acquisition must remain to distinguish this from the short-study item.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: All options gather specific diagnostic evidence. The task names the actual upcoming phase but no preferred investigation. There is no single cautious option against two premature operations. No named missing test sentence.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three investigations before committing to an invasive pyloric strategy.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: The test measured emptying during opioid exposure and excess glucose; the subsequent improvement is evidence against treating that result as a fixed current phenotype. Then Obtain an interpretable current emptying measurement before a pylorus-specific selection test.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Hard predicted: an apparently technically complete study can distract from preparation and changing symptoms.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: The exposure record conflicts with the current untreated symptom course despite adequate imaging duration. If repeated properly prepared studies showed continuing delay despite optimized medical care, a pyloric distensibility assessment could become reasonable during specialist procedural evaluation.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.confounded-scan.pylorus: temptation Use a treatment-selection measurement before confirming the continuing physiology. Why not here: A pyloric measurement does not establish that the confounded emptying abnormality persists after reversible factors change. Reasonable counterfactual: Persistent, adequately established refractory gastroparesis leaves a pylorus-specific assessment question. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-confounders, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-four-hour.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.confounded-scan.anatomic: temptation Treat improvement as unreliable while reopening an adequately examined structural question. Why not here: The reviewed CT and endoscopy addressed an outlet lesion, and no new obstructive pattern is supplied. The unresolved discrepancy is physiologic test preparation and interval response. Reasonable counterfactual: New structural findings or an inadequate outlet examination reopen obstruction assessment. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-obstruction, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-confounders.

Full-sequence check: Standalone; no earlier explanation rehearses medication confounding or repeats the same acquisition objective.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-confounders, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-four-hour, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-obstruction. Patient: Priya Lane, 42, Female. Complaint: Persistent meal-related vomiting. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.prokinetic-after-reaction.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 42-year-old woman with objectively documented diabetic gastroparesis, attends clinic because vomiting persists despite dietary treatment.

Current update: An earlier emergency record describes painful neck twisting and sustained upward eye deviation soon after metoclopramide was started; the movements resolved after it was stopped and treated. The current ECG QTc is within the laboratory range, and medication reconciliation identifies no interacting QT-prolonging drug.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which medicine should be considered next to improve {patientName}'s gastric emptying?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Oral erythromycin [KEY] ? Erythromycin is an offered prokinetic alternative. The earlier movement reaction precludes another metoclopramide trial; current QT/interaction assessment remains necessary.
2. Oral metoclopramide ? The prior reaction is compatible with acute dystonia, which contraindicates metoclopramide reuse.
3. Oral ondansetron ? Antiemetic symptom control does not address the requested gastric-emptying objective.

Explanation: Interpret the prior neck and eye movements as a metoclopramide-associated dystonic reaction and avoid re-exposure. Erythromycin is an alternative prokinetic to consider after safety review; an antiemetic addresses a different target. No dose or long-term regimen is implied.

Reasoning 1: Recognize the prior movement pattern and drug relationship rather than consider it a resolved nonspecific intolerance. Reasoning 2: Avoid the contraindicated prokinetic and choose an alternative that addresses emptying rather than nausea alone.

Closest error: metoclopramide. Deciding observation: The prior event began after metoclopramide and involved sustained neck/eye movements; the current goal is emptying. Consequence: Re-exposure can reproduce a serious movement adverse effect; symptom-only treatment can miss the requested physiologic target.

Counterfactual: Without a prior dystonic event or other contraindication, metoclopramide could be an appropriate initial prokinetic; the present alternative ranking would no longer be unique. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.prokinetic-reaction.metoclopramide. Deletion: Remove the reaction and two prokinetics become defensible; remove QT/interaction review and erythromycin safety is insufficiently specified.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Three parallel drug names; none contains the desired mechanism. The movement pattern replaces an authored diagnosis label. The task's emptying goal is necessary to distinguish an antiemetic from a prokinetic, not a unique label match.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three medication choices for the current target after nutrition intervention.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: Recognize the prior movement pattern and drug relationship rather than consider it a resolved nonspecific intolerance. Then Avoid the contraindicated prokinetic and choose an alternative that addresses emptying rather than nausea alone.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate/hard predicted: identify a historical adverse event and distinguish motor from nausea targets.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: The prior event began after metoclopramide and involved sustained neck/eye movements; the current goal is emptying. Without a prior dystonic event or other contraindication, metoclopramide could be an appropriate initial prokinetic; the present alternative ranking would no longer be unique.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.prokinetic-reaction.metoclopramide: temptation Choose the familiar approved prokinetic while dismissing a resolved event. Why not here: The prior reaction is compatible with acute dystonia, which contraindicates metoclopramide reuse. Reasonable counterfactual: Gastroparesis requires a prokinetic and no contraindication or prior dystonic/TD event is present. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.metoclopramide-dystonia, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.metoclopramide-reaction.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.prokinetic-reaction.ondansetron: temptation Treat vomiting and gastric motor delay as the same medication target. Why not here: Antiemetic symptom control does not address the requested gastric-emptying objective. Reasonable counterfactual: Nausea relief is the remaining target while a separate nutrition/motility plan is addressed. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-prokinetic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-antiemetic-target.

Full-sequence check: Standalone; no prior explanation supplies the reaction diagnosis or the alternative drug.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-prokinetic, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.metoclopramide-dystonia, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.metoclopramide-reaction, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.gp-antiemetic-target. Patient: Caleb Stone, 61, Male. Complaint: Bleeding record review. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.current-ulcer-risk.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old man, attends clinic to review a recent outside admission for melena. A separate admission last year required clipping of a bleeding ulcer.

Current update: During this admission, irrigation exposed a shallow duodenal ulcer with a dark mark level with the base. No projection or blood stream remained. No hemostatic intervention was performed. Subsequent hemoglobin measurements were unchanged, and oral intake resumed.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which acid-suppression plan best fits {patientName}'s current admission findings?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Scheduled oral omeprazole for ulcer healing [KEY] ? The current flat finding and stable course do not call for an intensive post-hemostasis course simply because last year's ulcer required clipping. An active ulcer still needs healing treatment.
2. High-dose pantoprazole during monitored post-hemostasis care ? That course follows treatment of high-risk ulcer stigmata; the current procedure did not show or treat such a lesion.
3. Scheduled oral famotidine for ulcer treatment ? A less intensive setting does not remove the indication for the PPI-based ulcer-healing plan offered here.

Explanation: Classify the current endoscopic observation: a flat pigmented mark differs from a protruding vessel. The prior admission does not determine today's stigma or require a new post-hemostasis PPI course. Provide oral ulcer-healing therapy in the stable represented course.

Reasoning 1: The mark is level with the base after irrigation, not a nonbleeding protruding vessel. Reasoning 2: Use ulcer-healing PPI treatment rather than inherit high-risk post-hemostasis care from a different episode.

Closest error: intensive-ppi. Deciding observation: The current endoscopic geometry and stable subsequent course differ from the prior clipped-ulcer episode. Consequence: Misclassification can cause unnecessary invasive/intensive treatment or undertreatment of an actual high-risk lesion.

Counterfactual: If this admission instead documented a protruding vessel treated endoscopically, the initial high-dose PPI course would be appropriate. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.current-low-risk-course.intensive-ppi. Deletion: Deleting the current procedure record makes the older clipping history dominate; deleting last year's history removes the intended episode-anchoring error.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: All options are specific acid-suppression courses. The task does not use low risk or name the favored route. Flat geometry is indispensable clinical evidence rather than an authored classification.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Current ulcer-directed acid suppression after the actual EGD course.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: The mark is level with the base after irrigation, not a nonbleeding protruding vessel. Then Use ulcer-healing PPI treatment rather than inherit high-risk post-hemostasis care from a different episode.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted: separate a previous high-risk event from present stigmata. Independent review should challenge whether the episode comparison adds sufficient resident difficulty.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: The current endoscopic geometry and stable subsequent course differ from the prior clipped-ulcer episode. If this admission instead documented a protruding vessel treated endoscopically, the initial high-dose PPI course would be appropriate.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.current-low-risk-course.intensive-ppi: temptation Treat a prior clipped ulcer or the word melena as an enduring high-risk stigma. Why not here: That course follows treatment of high-risk ulcer stigmata; the current procedure did not show or treat such a lesion. Reasonable counterfactual: The current admission requires successful hemostasis of a high-risk ulcer and its initial PPI course. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-high-risk, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-ppi.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.current-low-risk-course.h2: temptation Conflate no local hemostasis requirement with no need for the preferred ulcer-directed acid suppression. Why not here: A less intensive setting does not remove the indication for the PPI-based ulcer-healing plan offered here. Reasonable counterfactual: A clinician establishes a separate reason for an H2-based acid plan, such as inability to use a PPI; that constraint is not supplied here. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-healing-ppi.

Full-sequence check: Standalone; no earlier explanation labels the current ulcer.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-low-risk, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-healing-ppi, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-high-risk, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-ppi. Patient: Diane West, 64, Female. Complaint: Endoscopy record review. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.multiple-ulcer-sites.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside admission for melena. The admission endoscopy documented three ulcer sites after lavage.

Current update: In the gastric body, a dark dot lay level with the ulcer floor. In the antrum, pale fibrin covered an even ulcer floor. In the duodenal bulb, a rounded red projection persisted above the ulcer floor after irrigation. The field at each site remained dry.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which treatment should the endoscopist have performed for {patientName}'s recorded findings?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Place hemostatic clips at the duodenal-bulb focus [KEY] ? A persisting protruding vessel remains a high-risk stigma despite the dry field. The other described sites lack that finding.
2. Place hemostatic clips at the gastric-body focus ? The body finding is flat after lavage. Its dark color does not give it the same significance as a protruding vessel.
3. Place hemostatic clips at the gastric-antral focus ? A fibrin-covered even base without a vessel or flow is not the high-risk target described in this record.

Explanation: Use the relationship to the ulcer floor, not color or the absence of current flow. The duodenal-bulb projection represents the offered target requiring hemostasis. Keep the gastric sites and duodenal site distinct.

Reasoning 1: Distinguish the raised nonbleeding focus from two low-risk base appearances. Reasoning 2: Localize the consequential hemostatic action to the correct site.

Closest error: body. Deciding observation: A projection persists above the duodenal floor; the gastric dark mark is level with its floor. Consequence: Treating the wrong site leaves the high-risk vessel untreated while exposing another lesion to an unnecessary procedure.

Counterfactual: Swap the body and duodenal geometric observations, keeping the labels and dry field unchanged, and the gastric-body treatment becomes correct. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.ulcer-treatment-target.body. Deletion: Without the level-versus-raised observations, color and anatomical labels cannot establish the best target.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Every site has an observation; all options name the same action at one site and use parallel lengths. No protected image is promised. The prose record is the actual exhibit; a diagnosis label is withheld without withholding necessary geometry.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three site-specific local-hemostasis actions during the same endoscopy.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: Distinguish the raised nonbleeding focus from two low-risk base appearances. Then Localize the consequential hemostatic action to the correct site.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted; tests record interpretation and wrong-site risk rather than an abstract high-risk label. Residual recognition simplicity is flagged for independent review.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: A projection persists above the duodenal floor; the gastric dark mark is level with its floor. Swap the body and duodenal geometric observations, keeping the labels and dry field unchanged, and the gastric-body treatment becomes correct.

Patient: Arthur Bell, 69, Male. Complaint: Ulcer medication review. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.posthemostasis-ppi-course.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old man, attends clinic for a chart review of acid-suppression treatment during a recent hospital admission for duodenal-ulcer bleeding.

Current update: The admission EGD documented spurting from the ulcer, stopped with injection and clipping. A later EGD showed the clips in place with a dry base. At that point, only one day of the initial post-hemostasis PPI course had been completed and there was no new bleeding.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which medication plan should have been continued at this point in {patientName}'s hospital course?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Continue the initial high-dose pantoprazole course [KEY] ? The indication is the treated high-risk lesion and its initial post-hemostasis phase. A dry later view does not erase that treatment history.
2. Change to a standard-dose omeprazole healing course ? That is an appropriate later stage but downstages the represented initial post-hemostasis phase prematurely.
3. Change to a scheduled famotidine healing course ? A dry endoscopic field does not replace the supported post-hemostasis PPI indication with an H2-based strategy.

Explanation: The index spurting lesion was successfully treated, and only one day of the initial high-dose PPI phase had elapsed. Continue that initial phase, supported for 72 hours, rather than classify the ulcer solely from the later dry view. Accepted high-dose delivery regimens need not all be continuous infusion.

Reasoning 1: The later dry base documents treatment response, not low-risk pretreatment stigmata. Reasoning 2: Retain the initial post-hemostasis PPI course before moving to ulcer-healing intensity.

Closest error: standard. Deciding observation: Spurting required successful hemostasis and only one day of the initial course has elapsed. Consequence: Mistaking response for original risk can prematurely discontinue a supported protective treatment phase.

Counterfactual: After completion of the initial high-dose course, a clinically appropriate oral ulcer-healing course becomes reasonable. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.initial-ppi-course.standard. Deletion: Remove either the original spurting/hemostasis record or the elapsed course stage and the current dry view cannot establish the required intensity.

Author gate 1 / cue attack: Three medication courses have parallel labels. The history does not announce that PPI was omitted. A known treated lesion is needed for the regimen task; current absence of bleeding is necessary response evidence, not a safety giveaway.

Author gate 2 / stage and category: Three acid-suppression courses at a defined post-hemostasis stage.

Author gate 3 / consequential reasoning: The later dry base documents treatment response, not low-risk pretreatment stigmata. Then Retain the initial post-hemostasis PPI course before moving to ulcer-healing intensity.

Author gate 4 / predicted difficulty: Moderate predicted: distinguish pretreatment risk from observed treatment response and course completion.

Author gate 5 / single best and counterfactual: Spurting required successful hemostasis and only one day of the initial course has elapsed. After completion of the initial high-dose course, a clinically appropriate oral ulcer-healing course becomes reasonable.

- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.initial-ppi-course.standard: temptation Treat a later dry view as though the index ulcer had always been low risk. Why not here: That is an appropriate later stage but downstages the represented initial post-hemostasis phase prematurely. Reasonable counterfactual: The initial high-dose course is complete or the index lesion had low-risk stigmata without hemostasis. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-ppi, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-healing-ppi.
- Distractor choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.initial-ppi-course.h2: temptation Assume procedural success makes acid-suppression intensity or class unimportant. Why not here: A dry endoscopic field does not replace the supported post-hemostasis PPI indication with an H2-based strategy. Reasonable counterfactual: A separately justified non-PPI acid strategy is needed; no such constraint appears in this record. Claims: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-ppi.

Full-sequence check: Standalone; the low-risk case is not a preceding scored companion. No feedback reveals another item's regimen.

Evidence: claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-high-risk, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-ppi, claim.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.bleed-healing-ppi. Field/choice mappings: JSON proposals[].statementMapping and source ledger statementMappings. Clinical boundary: No claim that pantoprazole is uniquely superior to another accepted high-dose PPI or that the later EGD is routine care.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside admission for gastric-ulcer bleeding. Before admission he took aspirin after a documented myocardial infarction.

Current update: Endoscopic ulcer hemostasis was achieved. The discharge record documents recovery without further bleeding; aspirin had been stopped during the admission. There is no coronary stent or second antiplatelet medicine in his record.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which discharge medication plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded aspirin indication and ulcer course?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Resume aspirin with PPI gastroprotection [KEY] ? The aspirin indication is secondary cardiovascular prevention. After control, it should not remain withheld until complete ulcer healing; PPI protection addresses recurrent-ulcer risk.
2. Withhold aspirin until endoscopic ulcer healing ? Waiting for full healing disregards the secondary-prevention indication after a recovered bleeding course.
3. Substitute clopidogrel with PPI gastroprotection ? The record supplies no indication to change antiplatelet agents. The supported ulcer-bleeding recommendation preserves the indicated aspirin rather than automatically substitute another agent.

Explanation: The prior infarction establishes secondary prevention, and hemostasis has been achieved. Resume the indicated aspirin with PPI protection rather than wait for complete healing or change agents solely from the ulcer history. This item does not prescribe an exact restart day.

Reasoning 1: Distinguish secondary prevention after infarction from an optional preventive medication, then use the achieved hemostasis/current course. Reasoning 2: Restore the indicated aspirin while addressing ulcer protection.

Closest error: withhold. Deciding observation: A documented prior infarction provides an ongoing indication after controlled bleeding. Consequence: Unnecessarily prolonged interruption exposes the patient to avoidable thrombotic risk.

Counterfactual: If review instead showed no secondary-prevention indication, withholding aspirin for reassessment would become reasonable; that would be a different prescribing question. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.secondary-prevention-aspirin.withhold. Deletion: Without the actual aspirin indication, the balance is ambiguous. Without achieved control/current recovery, the discharge-phase recommendation cannot be assumed.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for sudden upper abdominal pain. The chart review follows the investigation and source-control decisions during that admission.

Current update: At presentation, pain began abruptly after several weeks of epigastric discomfort. Examination recorded upper abdominal guarding and pain with movement. The upright chest radiograph showed no subdiaphragmatic free air. Blood pressure was maintained during initial treatment.

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. CT of the abdomen and pelvis [KEY] ? Persistent clinical concern remains despite the radiograph. CT can assess a gastroduodenal leak and other causes of the acute abdominal findings.
2. Water-soluble upper gastrointestinal contrast study ? A contrast study has a selected role when a suspected leak remains unresolved, but CT is the recommended next examination in this initial radiograph-negative acute evaluation.
3. Upper endoscopy with gastric and duodenal inspection ? A possible free perforation is not an uncomplicated-ulcer mucosal evaluation. This study does not replace the recommended cross-sectional assessment of the acute extraluminal question.

Explanation: A plain radiograph without visible free air does not settle suspected perforation. Persistent acute guarding and pain with movement require interpretation of that limitation; CT addresses the remaining acute abdominal question.

Reasoning 1: The negative plain film has not explained an abrupt peritoneal-pattern presentation. Reasoning 2: Choose the appropriate next imaging investigation rather than downgrade to a mucosal-ulcer workup.

Closest error: contrast. Deciding observation: Acute guarding remains unexplained after a plain radiograph; no CT has yet supplied cross-sectional evidence. Consequence: Misreading the plain film can delay recognition and control of a leak.

Counterfactual: If CT were equivocal and clinical suspicion persisted for a small or sealed gastroduodenal leak, a water-soluble contrast study could become reasonable. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-imaging.contrast. Deletion: Remove the acute examination and outpatient mucosal workup becomes plausible; remove the actual prior modality and the next imaging stage is unclear.

Patient: James Porter, 57, Male. Complaint: Perforation admission review. Finite profile: profile.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-record.v1.

Presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, attends clinic after a hospital admission for sudden upper abdominal pain. The chart review follows the investigation and source-control decisions during that admission.

Prior visible sequence (must be considered with this task):
- question.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.perforation-imaging.v1: At presentation, pain began abruptly after several weeks of epigastric discomfort. Examination recorded upper abdominal guarding and pain with movement. The upright chest radiograph showed no subdiaphragmatic free air. Blood pressure was maintained during initial treatment. Task: Which investigation should the hospital have arranged next for {patientName}'s acute abdominal findings? Feedback: A plain radiograph without visible free air does not settle suspected perforation. Persistent acute guarding and pain with movement require interpretation of that limitation; CT addresses the remaining acute abdominal question.

Current update: CT showed contrast beyond the duodenal bulb with adjacent gas and fluid. After resuscitation, diagnostic laparoscopy found an 8 mm anterior bulb defect with edges that held sutures. No outlet narrowing or mass was seen; blood pressure remained maintained without vasoactive support.

Exhibits: No separate asset promised; the original constructed clinical record is supplied in the update.

Complete task: **Which source-control operation best fits {patientName}'s operative findings?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

1. Primary suture repair with peritoneal lavage [KEY] ? The small viable defect and maintained physiology support primary repair. The record does not establish a need for a larger resection or diversion.
2. Distal gastrectomy with gastrojejunal reconstruction ? This is a more extensive operation than the represented small anterior duodenal defect requires.
3. Pyloric exclusion with gastrojejunal bypass ? The viable small defect and absence of a narrowing or complex local disruption do not establish a need for diversion.

Explanation: The measured small defect, suture-holding edges and maintained physiology support primary repair. Do not make a routine omental patch mandatory: the guideline does not establish that it adds protection in every small perforation. Larger or complex defects require a different, individualized operation.

Reasoning 1: Identify a small directly repairable duodenal defect, rather than a large gastric or complex duodenal disruption. Reasoning 2: Select a source-control operation proportional to that anatomy and current physiology.

Closest error: exclusion. Deciding observation: The anterior bulb defect is 8 mm, holds sutures, and has no mass or outlet narrowing. Consequence: An unnecessary diversion/resection adds operative burden; inappropriate primary closure of a complex defect would be a different error.

Counterfactual: A large friable duodenal disruption with anatomy unsuitable for primary repair could make a tailored exclusion/diversion plan reasonable, pending specialist judgment. Choice: choice.topic.stomach-ulcer-bleeding-motility.small-duodenal-repair.exclusion. Deletion: Without size, tissue quality and site, the repair-versus-diversion choice is underdetermined. The physiologic response constrains the operative context.
